Q45: Under Article 13(2)–(3) of the EU AI Act, the provider must accompany the high-risk AI system with instructions for use that give deployers concise, complete, correct and clear information enabling them to interpret and properly use the system's output. These instructions must identify the provider (and, where applicable, its authorised representative) together with their contact details, and must describe the system's intended purpose along with any known or foreseeable circumstances of use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that could give rise to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. They must also specify the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14, including the technical means put in place to help deployers interpret the system's outputs. Additionally, the instructions must state the computational and hardware resources needed to run the system, its expected lifetime, and the maintenance and care measures (including their frequency) necessary to keep it functioning properly, including software updates. Finally, where relevant, they must describe the mechanisms built into the system that allow deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs generated in accordance with Article 12.
Q96: Annex III of the AI Act enumerates eight areas of high-risk use cases: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare decision making as such is not a standalone listed area, though healthcare-related applications are captured only where they fall within one of these categories - for example, AI systems used to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare services, systems used for risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, and emergency healthcare patient triage systems. Outside of these specifically enumerated touchpoints, general healthcare decision-making tools are not designated as high-risk under Annex III.
Q17: Yes, the Commission may adopt delegated acts under Article 97 to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems, but only where two conditions are both satisfied. First, the AI system in question must be intended for use in one of the areas already listed in Annex III. Second, the AI system must pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III. Both of these conditions must be met cumulatively for the Commission to exercise this power; satisfying only one is not sufficient.
Q74: Because your AI-generated audio is part of an evidently artistic and creative work, the full transparency obligation under Article 50(4) is scaled back specifically for this reason: you are not required to mark or disclose the content in any manner that would hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. However, this exception does not eliminate the disclosure duty entirely - you must still disclose, in some appropriate manner, that the audio content has been artificially generated or manipulated, so that its existence as AI-generated content is made known without interfering with how the work is experienced. In practice, this means choosing a disclosure format (such as a credit, label, or note accompanying the work) that flags the deepfake nature of the audio without being intrusive to the artistic presentation itself.
Q95: Under Article 6(2), Annex III organizes high-risk AI systems into distinct fields of application, referred to as "areas," each of which corresponds to a numbered heading in Annex III such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Within each area, Annex III then specifies one or more particular "use cases," meaning discrete, specifically described applications or purposes for which an AI system may be deployed, such as recruitment and selection within the employment area or evaluation of creditworthiness within the essential services area. In other words, each area functions as a category that contains one or more use cases falling within it, and it is these individual use cases that trigger high-risk classification for a given AI system. Annex III currently sets out eight such areas in total.
Q104: Annex X sets out a list of Union legal acts that establish the large-scale IT systems in the area of freedom, security and justice, covering the Schengen Information System, the Visa Information System, Eurodac, the Entry/Exit System, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN, and the interoperability framework Regulations. This list identifies which AI systems, by virtue of being components of those large-scale IT systems, fall within the special transitional regime of Article 111(1) rather than the general timelines applicable to other high-risk AI systems. Under that regime, AI components of an Annex X system already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 must be brought into compliance with the Regulation by 31 December 2030, and the Regulation's requirements must in the meantime be factored into each such system's periodic evaluation under its own founding legal act. In short, Annex X operates as the reference list that determines both the scope of this delayed compliance track and the specific deadlines attached to it.
